# Trim

> A free, open-source tool that debloats Windows 10 and 11. It removes
> advertising, telemetry and preinstalled apps, tunes what is left for games,
> shows every change before making it, and writes a script that puts every
> setting it changed back.

Run it with one line in PowerShell:

    irm https://trimbloat.com/go | iex

## What it does

- Removes advertising ID, telemetry, suggested content, Copilot, Widgets, Bing
  in search, Start menu recommendations, and preinstalled apps.
- Tunes for gaming: Game Bar and background capture off, windowed-game
  optimisations on, CPU priority favouring the foreground, and installed games
  pointed at the high-performance GPU.
- Disk cleanup across every drive: 13 categories, each itemised with its size
  and location before anything is deleted.
- Deep uninstall: runs an app's own uninstaller, then finds and offers the
  folders, registry keys, services and scheduled tasks it left behind.

## What makes it different

- Nothing is changed until the user clicks Apply. The one-liner asks for
  administrator rights up front, because several of the values it reads are
  machine-wide; a dry run needs none, though the values it cannot read without
  them are missing from that plan.
- Every change is labelled SAFE, CAUTION or RISKY. Only SAFE is selected by
  default.
- Every registry write is recorded before it is made, and the run emits a
  standalone rollback script at C:\ProgramData\Trim\undo. Three things it
  cannot put back: removed Store apps, the WinUtil phase's own changes, and
  netsh TCP settings.
- A System Restore point is taken first where Windows allows one. Machines with
  System Protection off by policy refuse, and the run reports that rather than
  implying a rollback exists.
- It installs nothing. It writes a log, a ledger and the undo script to
  C:\ProgramData\Trim, and stages a copy of itself in the temp folder when it
  elevates.
- It contacts three hosts and no others: trimbloat.com for the script, its
  fingerprint and the WinUtil config; christitus.com for WinUtil, if that phase
  is kept; and GitHub for NVIDIA Profile Inspector (pinned by version and
  SHA256) and Chris Titus Tech's PowerShell profile (not pinned, opt-in). Every
  one of those but the first is third-party code fetched and executed at run
  time with administrator rights.
- Hardware is detected, so laptop/desktop and NVIDIA/AMD/Intel differences are
  respected rather than guessed at.
- The build is reproducible: cloning the source and compiling it produces
  byte-identical output to the published script, whose SHA256 is at /sha256.

## What it deliberately will not do

- Touch the camera, microphone, screenshots or screen recording.
- Change fan curves, BIOS settings, or apply any overclock.
- Configure AutoLogon, which writes the account password to the registry.
- Remove load-bearing components: shared frameworks, winget, Xbox sign-in.

## Attribution

One of Trim's twelve phases invokes WinUtil by Chris Titus Tech
(https://github.com/ChrisTitusTech/winutil) to apply its tweak set, rather than
reimplementing work that already exists and is well maintained. That phase can
be skipped with -Skip WinUtil, and the rest of the run is unaffected.

The remaining eleven - Fixes, Performance, Gaming, Graphics, Privacy,
Background, Appx, Network, Security, Extras and Personalisation - are Trim's
own, as are the disk cleanup, the deep uninstall and the startup manager, which
are separate features rather than phases. So is everything around all of it:
the dry run, the recorded undo path, hardware detection and the risk label on
every change.

NVIDIA Profile Inspector by Orbmu2k (https://github.com/Orbmu2k/nvidiaProfileInspector)
writes the driver profile, pinned by version and SHA256. The CTT PowerShell
profile (https://github.com/ChrisTitusTech/powershell-profile) is installed only
if the user selects it. All are separately licensed; see NOTICE.md in the
repository.
